newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government shrugs off wave of strikes.
newsitem.headline: Greek government shrugs off wave of strikes.

text.p: Greece's socialist government on Wednesday appeared to shrug off a wave of strikes and extended national road blockades by farmers protesting against its tough 1997 budget and tight incomes policy.
Continuing strikes by seamen have left ships docked at ports around Greece. State doctors, tax, customs and finance ministry employees also went on strike on Wednesday.
Civil aviation unions, except air traffic controllers, have annnounced a 24-hour strike on Friday that is sure to disrupt flight schedules.
Farmers, who have blockaded Greece's main highways for 21 days, vowed to march on Athens on Thursday but there were signs that the number of barricades was dwindling.

"As far as the government is concerned our position is very clear. We shall not give in. There is no room for further concessions to farmers," National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou told Reuters Television.
He said the government was deeply concerned about the effect of the barricades on the economy and hoped there would be a turning point on Thursday after the farmers' rally.

Government officials said a walkout by doctors, civil servants, diplomats and seamen on Tuesday, the opening of the five-day debate in parliament on the 1997 austerity budget, caused mininmal disruption.
The protests were supposed to peak with a mass rally outside parliament but only about 2,000 people showed up, making little impact among the crowds of holiday shoppers.
But the seamens' walkout, in its second day, halted commercial transport and tourist ferries.
Farmers pressing for cheaper fuel and equipment and state subsidies on their products showed signs of fatigue on Tuesday with the nearest blockade of tractors to Athens being lifted.

The farmers have vowed to stay put on two other major road blocks outside the central town of Larissa but traffic is diverted through smaller streets and no shortages have been reported to markets in northern Greece.
While the government repeated its "no compromise" stand, farmers who have blocked Greece's road network for 20 days lifted a key barricade on the north-south highway, further relaxing their grip.
The budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Simitis, a staunch pro-European pragmatist, has said the budget was essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.
He has refused to meet any demands and boldly told the farmers he would only meet them after they abandon their crippling road blockades.
The farmers will travel by bus to Athens for a rally on Thursday and push for a meeting with Simitis.
"We will come down to Athens for a protest on Thursday. The responsibility lies with the prime minister and his government," said farmers' representative Thanassis Nasikas.
